title: Microworlds: SHRDLU, ELIZA, Shakey
text:
CHAPTER 9. SYMBOLIC AI
SECTION 9.4. MICROWORLDS: ELIZA, SHRDLU AND SHAKEY

By the mid-1960s symbolic AI had working theorem provers, search algorithms and a good language (Lisp). The next step was to build systems that talked, understood and acted. Because the real world was far too complex, researchers built "microworlds": small, simplified domains in which a program could show complete, coherent behavior. Three systems from this era became famous: ELIZA, a chatbot that seemed to understand but did not; SHRDLU, which genuinely understood language within a tiny world of blocks; and Shakey, the first mobile robot to reason about its own actions. Together they show both the achievements of symbolic AI and why it did not scale, a lesson that shaped the AI winters (Chapter 11).

1. ELIZA (1964-1967)

Joseph Weizenbaum (1923-2008) developed ELIZA at MIT between 1964 and 1967. It was written in MAD-SLIP (Weizenbaum's list-processing extension of the MAD language) and ran under the CTSS time-sharing system on an IBM 7094. Weizenbaum described it in "ELIZA - A Computer Program for the Study of Natural Language Communication Between Man and Machine," Communications of the ACM, volume 9 (1966), pages 36-45.

How it worked. ELIZA had no model of meaning. It used a script of keyword-based rules. Each rule had:

  - a keyword with a priority (for example "mother," "always," "I am");
  - one or more decomposition patterns that split the input around the keyword;
  - reassembly templates that build a reply using pieces of the input.

Pronouns were swapped (I <-> you, my <-> your). If no keyword matched, it used content-free replies ("Please go on.") or returned to an earlier topic stored in memory.

A rule in the style of the DOCTOR script:

    keyword: "I am"
    decomposition: (* I am *)          -- * matches any words
    reassembly: "How long have you been [2]?"
                "Do you believe it is normal to be [2]?"

    Input:  "I am unhappy about my job"
    Output: "How long have you been unhappy about your job?"

The most famous script, DOCTOR, imitated a Rogerian psychotherapist, who mostly reflects the patient's statements back. Weizenbaum chose this because such a therapist can say almost nothing of substance and still seem appropriate: the human supplies the meaning.

The ELIZA effect. Weizenbaum was surprised and disturbed that people, including his secretary, attributed understanding and feeling to the program and wanted to talk with it privately. Some psychiatrists suggested that automated therapy could become practical. The tendency to read understanding into a system's fluent output became known as the ELIZA effect. Weizenbaum became one of the first major critics of AI, arguing in his 1976 book "Computer Power and Human Reason" that some tasks, such as judgment about human lives, should not be handed to computers whether or not they could do them.

The ELIZA effect is directly relevant to modern large language models (Chapter 19), whose fluency is vastly greater; the question of what, if anything, lies behind fluent text is a serious one. ELIZA's original MAD-SLIP source code was rediscovered in the MIT archives in 2021 and published.

2. SHRDLU (1968-1970)

Terry Winograd developed SHRDLU at MIT in 1968-1970 as his PhD work. (The name comes from "ETAOIN SHRDLU," the order of keys on Linotype typesetting machines, roughly ordered by letter frequency.) It was written in Lisp and Micro Planner, ran on a DEC PDP-6 with a graphics display, and was described in "Understanding Natural Language," Cognitive Psychology, volume 3 (January 1972), and in a book of the same name.

The world. SHRDLU's world was a simulated table with blocks, pyramids and boxes of various colors and sizes, and a simulated robot hand. The user typed English commands and questions; SHRDLU moved objects, answered questions and explained its actions. Its exchanges included things like the following (paraphrased from published transcripts):

    User: Pick up a big red block.
    SHRDLU: OK. (it first moves a block that was on top of it)
    User: Find a block which is taller than the one you are holding
          and put it into the box.
    SHRDLU: By "it" I assume you mean the block which is taller than
            the one I am holding. OK.
    User: What does the box contain?
    SHRDLU: The blue pyramid and the blue block.
    User: Why did you clear off that cube?
    SHRDLU: To put it on a large green cube. ...

It could resolve pronouns ("it," "that cube"), handle relative clauses, ask for clarification when a command was ambiguous, learn new words ("a steeple is a stack of two green cubes and a pyramid," in this spirit), and answer "why" questions by consulting its own record of goals and subgoals.

How it worked. SHRDLU combined:

  - a parser based on systemic grammar, written as procedures;
  - a semantic component that turned phrases into references to objects and into goals;
  - a deductive component in Micro Planner, a language for goal-directed reasoning (a simplified implementation of Carl Hewitt's Planner): "to achieve (ON A B), clear the top of A, clear the top of B, grasp A, move it";
  - a model of the world state, and a record of the goal tree.

Its central claim was that understanding requires integrating syntax, meaning and knowledge of the world, and that knowledge could be represented as procedures (procedural semantics).

Why it did not scale. Everything in SHRDLU depended on the world being small, closed and fully known: a few dozen objects, a handful of relations and actions, a vocabulary of a few hundred words. Expanding to the open-ended real world meant hand-coding an almost unlimited amount of knowledge, and the interactions between pieces of hand-written knowledge became unmanageable. Winograd himself later turned away from this approach; his 1986 book with Fernando Flores, "Understanding Computers and Cognition," criticized the assumptions of symbolic AI.

3. Shakey (about 1966-1972)

Shakey was developed at the Stanford Research Institute (SRI) from about 1966 to 1972 by a team including Charles Rosen, Nils Nilsson and Peter Hart. It was the first general-purpose mobile robot able to reason about its own actions. In 1970 Life magazine called it the "first electronic person." It is now displayed at the Computer History Museum in Mountain View, California, and the project received an IEEE Milestone in 2017.

Hardware. Shakey was a tall wheeled cart with a television camera, sonar range finders, "bump detector" whiskers for collision detection, on-board electronics and a radio antenna. The heavy computing was done by a separate, room-sized computer linked by radio. Shakey moved slowly and in a jerky way, hence its name. Its world was a set of rooms with large blocks and wedges, doors and ramps, painted and lit to help its vision.

Software layers. Shakey's architecture had layers, an idea that remains standard in robotics:

  - Low-level actions: roll a distance, turn an angle, pan and tilt the camera; with feedback from sensors.
  - Intermediate-level actions: navigate to a location, push a block to a point, go through a door, combining low-level actions with error recovery.
  - High-level planning: given a goal like "push the block from room 1 into room 2," construct a sequence of intermediate actions.

Key results. Shakey's project produced three ideas still used today:

  - A* search (Section 9.3) for path planning on its map.
  - The Hough transform, in the form generalized by Richard Duda and Peter Hart (1972) to detect lines in images: each edge point votes for all lines rho = x cos(theta) + y sin(theta) passing through it, and peaks in the (rho, theta) accumulator are lines. It is still taught in every computer vision course and used in lane detection.
  - The visibility graph method for shortest paths among polygonal obstacles: connect start, goal and obstacle corners whose straight connections are unobstructed; the shortest path lies along this graph.

STRIPS. Shakey's planner was STRIPS (Stanford Research Institute Problem Solver), by Richard Fikes and Nils Nilsson (1971). STRIPS represents the world state as a set of logical facts, and each action by:

  - preconditions: facts that must be true to apply it;
  - add list: facts that become true;
  - delete list: facts that become false.

Example:

    Action: Push(b, x, y)        push box b from x to y
      Preconditions: At(Shakey, x), At(b, x), Pushable(b)
      Add:           At(Shakey, y), At(b, y)
      Delete:        At(Shakey, x), At(b, x)

The planner searches for a sequence of actions that transforms the initial state into one satisfying the goal, using a means-ends strategy descended from GPS (Section 9.1). The add/delete representation sidesteps part of the "frame problem" (identified by McCarthy and Hayes in 1969): how to state everything that does not change when an action happens. In STRIPS, anything not in an action's delete list is assumed to stay true. This STRIPS model is the ancestor of PDDL, the standard language of the automated planning competitions, and of planners still used in robotics and logistics.

Execution monitoring. Plans fail in the real world: a block slips, a door is blocked. Shakey's PLANEX system stored plans in "triangle tables" that let the executor check at each step which part of the plan was still valid, skip steps that had become unnecessary, or replan. Closing the loop between plan and perception is a cybernetic idea (Section 7.1) applied at the symbolic level.

4. What the microworlds taught

The microworlds were real achievements: complete systems in which language, reasoning, perception and action worked together. But they also revealed problems that came to define the limits of the symbolic approach:

  - Scaling: methods that worked with 20 objects collapsed with thousands, through combinatorial explosion in search and the cost of hand-coding knowledge.
  - Brittleness: systems failed completely outside their designed domain; there was no graceful degradation.
  - The frame and qualification problems: specifying all effects and all preconditions of real actions is practically impossible.
  - Perception: vision in a carefully lit room with matte painted blocks did not transfer to cluttered real scenes. Hans Moravec later emphasized that the "low-level" skills of perception and movement, easy for a one-year-old child, were much harder for computers than the "high-level" reasoning of chess or algebra (Moravec's paradox).
  - Common sense: understanding ordinary language needs vast amounts of background knowledge about the world.

These problems, combined with over-optimistic predictions and funding pressure, fed into criticism such as the 1973 Lighthill report and the first AI winter (Chapter 11). They also prompted two different responses: putting enormous amounts of domain knowledge into expert systems (Chapter 12), and, much later, learning knowledge from data instead of writing it by hand (Chapters 13-19). In robotics, Rodney Brooks's behavior-based robots of the late 1980s rejected Shakey's central world model and planning in favor of layers of simple reactive behaviors, an echo of Grey Walter's tortoises (Section 7.3).

Modern robots combine both traditions: learned perception, classical state estimation and control, and planning with A*, sampling-based planners or STRIPS-like task planners, increasingly guided by large language models that translate instructions into goals, as SHRDLU's designers had hoped to do with hand-written grammars.

5. Summary

  - ELIZA (Weizenbaum, MIT, 1964-1967) used keyword patterns and reassembly templates; the DOCTOR script imitated a Rogerian therapist. People's readiness to attribute understanding is the ELIZA effect.
  - SHRDLU (Winograd, MIT, 1968-1970) understood English commands and questions about a blocks world by integrating parsing, semantics and procedural reasoning in Lisp and Micro Planner.
  - Shakey (SRI, about 1966-1972) was the first mobile robot to reason about its actions, with layered control; it produced A*, the Duda-Hart Hough transform, visibility graphs and the STRIPS planner.
  - STRIPS represents actions with preconditions, add lists and delete lists, the basis of modern planning languages.
  - Microworlds showed what symbolic AI could do and why it struggled to scale: brittleness, combinatorial explosion, the frame problem, perception and common sense.
